items.text: On September 28, Reuters reported on Anthropic's IPO prospectus, giving investors their first look at the company's finances. Revenue reached nearly $4.6 billion in 2025, a twelvefold increase from the prior year, alongside an operating loss exceeding $8 billion. The headline net loss of about $42 billion included a roughly $34 billion accounting charge tied to the rising estimated value of financing that could convert into shares, rather than operating spend. The prospectus also shows $518 billion in planned cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations, and nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue came from two customers. The reported target valuation is more than double the $965 billion mark set in May, which would make this the private-to-public repricing every AI lab investor is watching.

On September 28, AMD agreed to acquire World Labs, the San Francisco AI lab developing a world model, for $8.2 billion in an all-stock transaction. AMD was already an investor, and the deal is its second-largest on record after the roughly $50 billion Xilinx purchase. Closing is expected by year-end, subject to regulatory approval. It's the week's largest venture-backed exit, and another sign chipmakers are buying model capability rather than building it.

On September 29, Oura postponed its Nasdaq IPO, citing market uncertainty and giving no new date; it had aimed to raise up to $2.2 billion, at a valuation near $15 billion. The company said demand was strong, and the deal was reportedly about four times oversubscribed. Oura wasn't alone: Holtec Nuclear withdrew its IPO, Amaero postponed, and Bamboo Insurance postponed in the days before. For pre-IPO holders, it's a reminder that rising yields can close the window even for profitable issuers.

On September 28, Instinct, which is building a personal AI assistant for everyday tasks, raised a $1 billion Series C from Sequoia, Benchmark and Coatue at a $10 billion valuation, roughly a year after founding. It was the only $1B+ private round of the week, and a striking price for a consumer-agent company with no public comparable.

On October 1, AI-native cybersecurity company Armadin raised a $255.5 million Series B co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, at a valuation of over $2.5 billion, bringing total funding to $445 million. In-Q-Tel and GV were among returning backers, signaling that agentic security is drawing both government-adjacent and growth capital.
